I am 59 years old and have been farming these fields in Quzhou since I was a young girl. I never went to school, but I know this land better than anyone. My family has 8 mu, and I will plant winter wheat on all of it this autumn, just like always. After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize on the same 8 mu — that is what everyone in our village does, and the turnaround is so tight there is no time to waste.

For the wheat, I will use an improved variety like Shimai or Lumai — my neighbors do well with these, and the seed shop has them every year. I will rotary till the ground before sowing in mid-October. I buy one bag of compound fertilizer per mu for the base dressing, and I will topdress with extra nitrogen when the wheat turns yellow at jointing time. I irrigate three times: once before winter to help the wheat survive the cold, once in spring when it starts growing fast, and once when the grain is filling. I spray four times total — herbicide once, insecticide twice when I see aphids, and fungicide once if the weather turns wet.

For the maize, I plant hybrid seed — Nongda 372 or Denghai 605 — because hybrid maize grows fast and strong. There is no time to till between wheat harvest and maize planting, so we plant no-tillage directly into the wheat stubble. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, and irrigate twice — once right after sowing and once during the big growth period. I spray three times: herbicide once, insecticide twice for the corn borers.

I expect about 1000 jin of wheat per mu and 1100 jin of maize per mu, which is what I usually get when the weather cooperates. Some years I make a bit more, some years a bit less, but this system feeds my family and brings in cash from selling the extra grain.
